title: Biggest Lottery Winners: What Really Happened After
description: The jackpots are jaw-dropping. But the real stories of America's biggest lottery winners — who they were, what they chose, what changed — are far more human.
content:
The Night Everything Changed

Somewhere in the gap between checking a ticket and walking out of a lottery office, an ordinary life ends and something entirely new begins. It isn't the moment the numbers fall — it's the moment a person realizes those numbers are theirs. What happens in the hours, days, and years that follow tells us far more about human nature than any jackpot figure ever could. These are the true stories of some of the biggest lottery winners in American history — not just what they won, but who they were, and what the money actually did to their lives.

Section 1: Who Were These People Before the Win

Mavis Wanczyk was a hospital worker from Chicopee, Massachusetts. She had spent 32 years working at Mercy Medical Center, most recently in the patient care department. By August 2017, she was 53 years old — a mother and grandmother who, by her own account, had always dreamed of quitting her job someday. She was not a person defined by ambition for wealth. She was defined by routine, by showing up, by decades of quiet reliability.

Manuel Franco was 24 years old when his life changed in March 2019. He was a young man from West Allis, Wisconsin, working an ordinary job, living an ordinary life by any external measure. He was among the youngest winners of a major jackpot on record in the United States — a detail that would shape how the public received his story and how commentators interpreted his choices.

Then there were the three winning tickets in the January 2016 Powerball drawing — a jackpot that reached $1.586 billion, split among winners in California, Tennessee, and Florida. Those ticket holders were not celebrities. They were ordinary people who happened to be holding the right slip of paper on the right night. The winners from Tennessee — John and Lisa Robinson — went on the Today show the morning after the draw, still holding their ticket in a plastic sleeve, visibly overwhelmed. They looked like people who hadn't slept, because they hadn't.

Section 2: The Claim, the Chaos, and the First Decisions

Mavis Makes a Phone Call

Mavis Wanczyk's first documented act after confirming her $758.7 million Powerball jackpot — the largest ever won by a single ticket at that time — was to call her employer and quit. She made the call before she had even left the lottery office. "I just wanted to make that call," she told reporters at the press conference, smiling. It is one of the most purely human moments in lottery history: not a financial advisor, not a lawyer, not a press agent. A phone call to her boss.

She chose the lump sum cash option, which came to approximately $480 million before taxes. After federal and state taxes — Massachusetts taxes lottery winnings as regular income — her take-home figure was significantly lower. Anyone curious about how those tax layers work can run the numbers through a lottery tax calculator to understand what winners in different states actually pocket. Wanczyk was clear at her press conference that she planned to take care of her family first. She then, largely, disappeared from public life — a choice that many financial advisors consider wise, and that the public rarely gets to see executed so cleanly.

Manuel Franco and the Weight of Youth

When Manuel Franco stepped forward to claim his share of the $768.4 million Powerball jackpot in March 2019, he was 24 years old. He took the lump sum: approximately $477 million before taxes. At a press conference, he described the days between winning and claiming as among the most surreal of his life — he said he had felt physically ill with the stress of holding the secret. "The best days of my life," he said, then paused, "and the most frightening." Franco indicated he intended to travel, to help his family, and to give to charity, but kept further details private.

The 2016 Split and the Robinsons

The $1.586 billion Powerball jackpot from January 2016 remains the largest lottery prize in US history by advertised jackpot amount, split three ways among tickets in California, Tennessee, and Florida. The Tennessee winners, John and Lisa Robinson from Munford, made the unusual choice to go public almost immediately — appearing on national television within 24 hours of the draw. Their portion of the jackpot, after the three-way split and the lump sum election, still represented a generational sum. Their openness was striking in contrast to winners who retain anonymity; it gave the public a rare, unfiltered look at the disorientation of sudden, enormous wealth.

Section 3: The Longer Arc — What the Money Did and Didn't Do

Mavis Wanczyk's story, as far as the public record shows, is one of quiet withdrawal. She gave a single press conference, expressed her intentions simply, and was not heard from again in any significant public capacity. Whether that represents happiness or hardship, no one outside her circle can say — and that privacy itself seems deliberate. The absence of a troubled follow-up story is, in its own way, a kind of outcome.

The story of Jack Whittaker — who won a $314.9 million Powerball jackpot in December 2002 in West Virginia, then the largest single-ticket jackpot ever — went in a different direction. Whittaker was already a successful businessman before the win. What followed was extensively documented in public court records and news reports: lawsuits, theft of large sums from his vehicle, personal losses, and legal troubles that accumulated over years. Whittaker himself was quoted in multiple interviews saying the win had brought him more suffering than joy. His story is not a simple moral, but it is an honest one: money did not insulate him from grief, and in some ways accelerated it.

Gloria MacKenzie, who claimed a $590.5 million Powerball jackpot in May 2013 at age 84 — making her the oldest solo jackpot winner on record — chose the lump sum and kept almost entirely out of public view afterward. She had been living in a modest home in Zephyrhills, Florida. At 84, her story carried a different texture than younger winners: not a life transformed so much as a life's final chapter rewritten in comfort.

Section 5: The Most Human Moment

"I just wanted to take care of my family and be a recluse." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her August 2017 press conference after winning the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot

It is a sentence worth sitting with. Not a word about investment portfolios, real estate empires, or legacy projects. After 32 years of working a hospital job, Wanczyk's first articulated vision of her future was simple: family, and quiet. For many people, that is the whole dream. The dollar figure was almost incidental to what she actually wanted.

Section 6: What These Stories Tell Us, Without Judgment

Across all of these cases, a few patterns emerge — not rules, not cautionary tales, just observable things. Winners who moved quickly to retain legal and financial counsel before going public tended to maintain more control over what followed. Winners who chose anonymity where their state permitted it tended to have fewer documented conflicts in the years after. And winners who had a clear, simple sense of what they actually wanted — Wanczyk's "take care of my family and be a recluse" — seemed, at least from the outside, to navigate the transition with more clarity than those who didn't.

What the money reliably did: it eliminated financial constraint. What it did not reliably do: resolve pre-existing family tensions, guarantee personal happiness, or protect anyone from grief, illness, or loss. Jack Whittaker's experience is the most publicly documented example of this, but it is not unique in kind — only in the degree to which the details became public record. The biggest lottery winners in America are not a monolith. They are a cross-section of ordinary people handed an extraordinary variable and asked to navigate it without a map.

For anyone curious about how jackpots are structured, taxed, and distributed across different states, all state lottery guides offer a useful breakdown of the rules and tax environments that shape what a winner actually receives. The difference between winning in California and winning in Massachusetts, for example, is not trivial when the figures involved are in the hundreds of millions.

Section 7: Further Reading by State

Many of the stories above are rooted in specific state lottery systems, each with its own rules around anonymity, tax withholding, and claim deadlines. Winner stories are as much about the systems surrounding a jackpot — legal, financial, familial — as they are about the jackpot itself. Understanding those systems is part of understanding why the outcomes look so different from one winner to the next.
